34.1: THE GAMBLER'S SONG — told by the gambler himself. He says the dice, made from the nuts of a tree on a windy mountain, excite him as they roll on the board. He loves them even more than the best Soma. He is trapped by a habit.
34.2: Sadly he admits: 'My wife was always kind and never angry with me or my friends, but because of the dice I pushed her away.' Bad habits can hurt the people who love us most.
34.3: Now his wife keeps away from him and her mother dislikes him. Nobody comforts him. He feels as useless as an old, tired horse that nobody wants to buy.
34.4: Because he lost everything, even his own family says, 'We don't know him — take him away!' The habit has made him lose his place at home.
34.5: He decides, 'I won't play any more,' and his gambling friends leave him. But as soon as he hears the dice rattle, he runs back to them. Breaking a habit is very hard!
34.6: The gambler goes to the gambling hall with his heart burning, wondering, 'Will I win this time?' The dice keep him wanting more and more.
34.7: The dice are described as having hooks and goads (sharp sticks) that pull and hurt. They give small wins and then take everything — even from the one who seemed to be winning.
34.8: There are fifty-three dice playing together like a troop. They don't care about anyone's anger — even a king has to bow to them. A habit can rule even powerful people.
34.9: The dice roll down and jump up. They have no hands, but they make people with hands serve them. Cold themselves, they burn the heart to ashes like magic coals.
34.10: The gambler's wife is left sad and alone, his mother cries for her son who wanders without a home. In debt and afraid, he sneaks around at night.
34.11: He feels sad seeing other people's happy wives and tidy homes. He starts the day like everyone else, but by evening, when the fire is cold, he ends up alone and ashamed.
34.12: The gambler turns to the leader of the dice and holds up his ten fingers: 'I'm telling the truth — I have nothing left to hide.' He is finally ready to stop.
34.13: The famous lesson, given by the god Savitṛ: 'Don't play with dice! Plough your field! Enjoy what you earn and think it is enough. There are your cows, there is your wife.' Honest work and contentment bring happiness.
34.14: He says goodbye to the dice: 'Be my friends in a gentle way, don't attack me with your power. Let the dice trap someone else!' He is ready to start a new life.

75.1: THE RIVER SONG. The poet praises the greatness of the Waters. The rivers come in groups of seven, three times over — and the Sindhu (Indus) is the mightiest of all.
75.2: Varuṇa dug the riverbed so Sindhu could run like a racer. She rushes over the steep ridges of the land, leading all the other rivers.
75.3: Sindhu's roar rises up to the sky. She rushes with endless power and flashing light, like rain falling from thundering clouds, bellowing like a bull.
75.4: The other rivers run to Sindhu like mothers to their calves, like cows bringing milk. Sindhu leads them like a king leading the two wings of his army.
75.5: This verse is like a map! 'Accept my song, O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī (Sutlej), Paruṣṇī (Ravi), Asiknī (Chenab), Vitastā (Jhelum)...' The rivers are named from east to west.
75.6: Now the rivers that join the Sindhu from the west are named, like the Kubhā (Kabul river) and Gomatī. Sindhu flows together with all of them.
75.7: Sindhu shines and sparkles white in her power, carrying huge amounts of water across the land, the most active of all, beautiful like a spotted mare.
75.8: Sindhu is rich in good horses, chariots, cloth, gold and wealth. The young rivers Śīlamāvatī and Ūrṇāvatī are dressed in sweetness. Rivers bring riches to the land around them.
75.9: Sindhu has yoked her chariot pulled by horses and will win the race. The poet ends by praising her free, mighty, roaring power. People loved their rivers because rivers gave life.

90.1: The PURUṢA SUKTA. Imagine a giant cosmic being with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes and a thousand feet — 'thousand' means 'countless'. He covers the whole earth and reaches even beyond it.
90.2: The Puruṣa is everything that has been and everything that will be. He is the lord of immortality and keeps growing greater.
90.3: His greatness is huge, but he is even greater than that. All the creatures in the world are only one quarter of him; the other three quarters are beyond, in the immortal heaven.
90.4: Three quarters of the Puruṣa rose up high, and one quarter stayed here and spread out into everything — both things that eat (living beings) and things that don't.
90.5: From the Puruṣa came Virāj (the spread-out universe), and from Virāj the Puruṣa was born again, spreading east and west over the earth. Creation is shown as a circle.
90.6: The gods held a great ceremony using the Puruṣa himself as the offering. The seasons were part of it: spring was the ghee, summer the firewood, autumn the offering. Time itself joined the act of creation.
90.7: The gods, the Sādhyas and the rishis performed this first ceremony with the Puruṣa. It is a picture of the whole universe being made from one being — not a real event to copy.
90.8: From that great offering came the creatures of the air and the animals of the forest and the village.
90.9: From it were born the hymns of the Rigveda (Ṛcas), the songs (Sāmans), the meters and the Yajus formulas — the Vedas themselves come from the cosmic being.
90.10: From it came horses, cows, goats and sheep — all the animals.
90.11: Now the poet asks: when the Puruṣa was divided, how many parts were made? What became his mouth, his arms, his thighs and his feet?
90.12: The answer names four groups of society — priests, rulers, traders and workers — as coming from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet. People today discuss and debate this verse a lot, because it was later used to treat people as higher or lower. The hymn's bigger picture is that all parts belong to one body, and a body needs every part.
90.13: The Moon was born from his mind, the Sun from his eye, Indra and Agni from his mouth, and Vāyu (the wind) from his breath. Nature and our own bodies are linked.
90.14: The air came from his navel, the sky from his head, the earth from his feet and the directions from his ears. This is how the worlds were shaped.
90.15: The ceremony had seven boundary sticks and three times seven bundles of firewood. Seven and three are special numbers in the Vedas.
90.16: By this first offering the gods set up the first rules of worship and reached the highest heaven. The message: the whole universe is one living whole, and everything in it is connected.

97.1: THE HEALING PLANTS SONG, by a seer named Bhiṣag — which means 'doctor'! He says the plants were born long, long ago, even before the gods, and he will tell of their hundred and seven powers.
97.2: He calls the plants 'Mothers' with hundreds of homes and thousands of shoots. 'You who have a thousand powers, make this sick person well!'
97.3: 'Be happy with the plants that flower and bear fruit! They lead us to success like horses that win a race.'
97.4: 'Plants, I call you Mothers and Goddesses.' The healer hopes to bring the patient's own self back to health.
97.5: The plants live in the holy fig tree (aśvattha) and the parṇa tree. The healer promises they will be rewarded if they make the patient well.
97.6: The one who keeps many healing herbs ready, like a king among people, is called a 'physician' — someone who chases away disease.
97.7: The healer has gathered herbs full of strength and nourishment so the patient can become whole again.
97.8: The healing power of plants flows out like cows coming out of the barn, to save the patient's breath and life.
97.9: The plants are called 'Relievers' and 'Restorers'. They are like flowing rivers with wings, keeping disease far away.
97.10: The plants slip past every fence, like a thief sneaking into a cowshed — but this 'thief' steals away the sickness from the body!
97.11: When the healer holds the herbs in his hand, bringing back lost strength, the sickness runs away before it can harm the patient.
97.12: The plants move through the body, limb by limb and joint by joint, and push out disease like a strong judge ending a quarrel.
97.13: 'Fly away, sickness! Go with the blue jay and the kingfisher, rush away with the wind and the storm!'
97.14: 'Plants, help one another — work together like a team and support my words.' Teamwork, even among plants!
97.15: 'Plants with fruit and without, with flowers and without, sent by Bṛhaspati — free us from pain and sorrow.'
97.16: 'Free me from curses and from Varuṇa's punishment, from the noose of Yama (death), and from any wrong done against the gods.'
97.17: When the plants came down from the sky to the earth, they said: 'No harm will come to the person we enter while he is alive.'
97.18: Among all the plants, whose king is Soma, the healer praises one special plant as the best — quick to help and sweet to the heart.
97.19: 'All you herbs spread over the earth, whose king is Soma — put all your healing power together into this one plant.'
97.20: 'May the one who digs you up not be harmed, nor the person I dig you up for. May no sickness attack our people or our animals.' Even picking herbs is done with care and respect.
97.21: 'All plants who hear this, and those far away — come together and give your healing power to this herb.'
97.22: The plants speak to Soma, their king: 'We save from death the person whose cure is undertaken by a wise healer.'
97.23: 'You are the best of all plants, and the trees serve you.' This hymn shows an early love of medicine from nature — the roots of Āyurveda.

121.1: In the very beginning appeared Hiraṇyagarbha — the 'Golden Womb' or 'Golden Egg'. As soon as he was born, he became the one Lord of all beings and held up the earth and the sky. Each verse ends with the question: 'To which god shall we offer our worship?'
121.2: He gives breath, life and strength. All the gods follow his commands. Both immortality and death are like his shadow. 'To which god shall we offer our worship?'
121.3: By his greatness he became the only ruler of everything that breathes and sleeps, lord of people and animals. The question repeats — the poet is wondering out loud.
121.4: The snowy mountains (the Himalayas), the ocean and the far river Rasā all belong to him. The directions of the sky are like his arms.
121.5: Because of him the sky is strong and the earth is steady; he holds up the realm of light and measured out the space in between.
121.6: Two armies facing each other look up to him in fear, while the risen Sun shines over them. Everyone looks to the highest power in difficult times.
121.7: When the great waters came, carrying the seed of everything and giving birth to fire (Agni), the single life-breath of the gods arose. A picture of creation coming from waters and fire.
121.8: In his power he looked over the waters that held the force of creation. 'He is the god above the gods; there is no other.'
121.9: 'May he never harm us — the one who made the earth and the sky, whose laws are true, who brought the great shining waters.'
121.10: The answer at last: 'Prajāpati (Lord of all creatures)! Only you understand everything that has been created. Grant us what our hearts wish for.' The hymn's question leads to wonder about the one source of all.

125.1: The DEVĪ SUKTA, by the woman seer Vāk, daughter of the sage Ambhṛṇa. The goddess Vāk (Speech) speaks in her own voice: 'I travel with the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas and all the gods. I hold up Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Agni and the twin Aśvins.'
125.2: 'I support Soma, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan and Bhaga. I give wealth to the one who worships with devotion.' She is the power behind all the gods.
125.3: 'I am the Queen, the gatherer of treasures, the wisest, the first of those worthy of worship. The gods have placed me in many places.' Speech is everywhere — in every home and every heart.
125.4: 'Through me everyone eats, sees, breathes and hears what is said. People don't notice it, but they live with me. Listen to the truth I tell!' Without speech and understanding, we could not share or learn.
125.5: 'I myself speak the words that gods and people welcome. Whoever I love, I make strong, wise, a rishi.' Knowledge and good words can lift a person up.
125.6: 'I bend Rudra's bow so his arrow strikes those who hate goodness. I stir up the people to stand up for what is right, and I fill Earth and Heaven.'
125.7: 'I give birth to the Father at the top of the world; my home is in the waters, in the ocean. From there I spread over all beings and touch the sky with my forehead.'
125.8: 'I breathe out like the strong wind, holding all things together. I have grown so great — beyond this earth and beyond the heavens.' A powerful, confident song, still chanted in honour of the Goddess during Navarātri.

129.1: THE CREATION MYSTERY (Nāsadīya Sukta). Before everything, there was neither 'nothing' nor 'something'. No air, no sky. What covered it all? Where? Was there deep water? The poet begins with questions, not answers.
129.2: There was no death and no immortality, no sign of night or day. Only That One breathed, without air, by its own power. Nothing else existed.
129.3: Darkness was hidden in darkness; everything was a shapeless mixture. Then, by the great power of heat (tapas), the One was born.
129.4: Then came Desire — the first seed of mind and thought. Wise seers, searching in their hearts, found how 'what exists' is connected to 'what does not exist'.
129.5: A line was stretched across — what was above and what was below? There were seeds of life and great powers, energy below and force above. The poet imagines creation slowly taking shape.
129.6: 'Who really knows? Who can tell where this creation came from?' Even the gods came after the world began, so who knows how it all started? This is real scientific curiosity.
129.7: The amazing ending: the one who watches over the world from the highest heaven — he surely knows... or perhaps even he does not know! The Rigveda teaches that it is wise to admit when we are not sure.

146.1: THE FOREST LADY (Araṇyānī). 'Lady of the Forest, you seem to disappear as I look for you! Why don't you ask the way to the village? Aren't you afraid out there?'
146.2: When the grasshopper chirps and the cicada answers, as if ringing little bells, the Lady of the Forest is happy. The forest is full of music if you listen.
146.3: In the evening, it seems as if cows are grazing far away, as if there is a house over there, as if carts are being unhitched. The forest plays tricks on our eyes.
146.4: Someone seems to call a cow; someone else seems to chop a tree. At dusk a person in the forest thinks, 'Did somebody scream?' What seems scary is often just unfamiliar sounds.
146.5: The poet reassures us: the Forest Goddess never harms anyone unless an attacker comes. A person can eat sweet fruit there and rest as he likes.
146.6: 'I have praised the Forest Queen, smelling sweetly of balm, the Mother of all wild creatures, who has plenty of food without ploughing.' The forest feeds everyone freely — let us protect it.

191.1: The LAST hymn of the Rigveda. The book began with Agni, and its last hymn begins with Agni too: 'Mighty Agni, you gather all precious things for your friend. Bring us all treasures as you are kindled.'
191.2: The famous call for unity: 'Walk together, speak together, let your minds agree — just as the gods of old shared their portions in harmony.' Many schools and meetings in India begin with this verse.
191.3: 'Let your meeting place be common, your gathering common, your mind and thoughts united. I give you a shared purpose; worship together with a shared offering.'
191.4: The closing verse (missing from Griffith's translation): 'Let your intentions be the same, your hearts the same, your minds the same, so that you may live happily together.' The Rigveda ends with a wish for all people to live in harmony.
